title: Shannon-metered inline rANS coding in the memory controller
idea: First principles: a byte of typical server heap carries only ~2-4 bits of Shannon entropy, so storing 8 bits is pure waste. Put a table-driven rANS (asymmetric numeral system) codec in the memory controller, with frequency tables per page class learned online by a sampling engine; 4 KB pages live in variable-size 512 B sub-blocks tracked by a small translation table, and hot lines are cached decompressed.
why: Capacity per installed bit: 1.8-2.5x effective DRAM on heaps and caches, measured against the entropy bound, for ~5-10 ns of decode on misses; cuts the DRAM bought per server directly.

title: Entropy-sized pointers: hardware 32-bit region-relative pointer storage
idea: A 64-bit pointer inside a heap carries only log2(reachable objects), about 28-34 bits of information. The allocator sets a per-page pointer-map bit; the memory controller stores tagged words as 32-bit offsets from a per-1 GB region base held in page metadata and re-expands them on load.
why: Pointer-dense workloads (graphs, JVM/Go heaps, key-value stores, B-trees) are 30-50% pointers; halving them saves 15-25% of DRAM at ~1 cycle of expand latency.

title: Exponent-dictionary storage for BF16 and FP8 tensors
idea: Measured from the data, the 8-bit exponent field of trained BF16 weights and activations holds only ~2.5-3 bits of entropy because values cluster within a few octaves. Logic on the HBM/CXL base die stores each 128-value block as 3-bit codes into a per-block 8-entry exponent palette plus raw sign and mantissa, with a raw fallback for outlier blocks.
why: Lossless ~1.4x smaller tensors (16 bits to ~11.4 bits per value) with bit-exact results, so a model that needed 8 HBM stacks fits in 6.

title: Joule-and-dollar ledger deciding store versus recompute per tensor
idea: Price every resident object by its physical rent: capacity amortization ($/GB-s) plus refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit per 64 ms), against the energy and time to rebuild it from its inputs (FLOPs x ~0.5 pJ). A runtime keeps a lineage graph, like Spark or autograd, and drops any tensor, query intermediate or memo entry whose rebuild cost is below its rent, extending activation checkpointing to all data.
why: 30-60% smaller footprint for training activations, analytics intermediates and memo caches, because energy per FLOP has fallen ~10x faster than DRAM cost per bit.

title: Store KV cache as token IDs plus sparse anchors
idea: A token is ~17 bits of information, but its KV cache in a 70B-class model is ~160-320 KB, an expansion of ~100,000x. Keep only token IDs and a full KV snapshot every 64 tokens (anchors); on access, regenerate the missing span's KV with a batched prefill from the nearest anchor on tensor cores that sit idle during memory-bound decode.
why: KV capacity falls ~30-60x for long contexts and parked sessions. The price is ~1.2-2x extra prefill FLOPs, paid from compute that is otherwise stranded.

title: Attention-mass bit-plane decay for KV entries
idea: The information an entry must keep scales with the attention it receives: an entry with cumulative softmax weight 1e-4 needs only a few bits. Store KV in bit-plane-major layout and, as a per-token running attention-mass counter decays, free the lowest bit planes in place (16 to 8 to 4 to 2 bits), so precision degrades gracefully instead of tokens being evicted.
why: 3-6x KV capacity at near-lossless quality; freeing whole planes needs no rewrite or compaction.

title: Stack-distance profiler sizing each VM's DRAM to its miss-curve knee
idea: The minimum DRAM a workload needs is set by its reuse-distance distribution, not its allocation. A hardware Mattson stack-distance sampler in the memory controller (hashed address sampling with a small SHARDS-style tree) builds each VM's miss-ratio curve in real time; the hypervisor grants local DRAM up to the knee and backs the tail with compressed or CXL memory.
why: Servers carry 25-40% more DRAM than the measured knee; sizing to it cuts purchases ~20-30% at <2% slowdown.

title: Rack-level spot market for gigabyte-seconds of pooled memory
idea: Treat DRAM as a perishable flow (GB-s), not a stock. Each rack's CXL memory pool runs a second-by-second auction in which jobs bid for leases that carry an eviction penalty, and the scheduler packs the bids so pooled DRAM runs at 85-90% utilization instead of the 50-60% of statically provisioned servers.
why: Recovers most of the 25-40% stranded memory in clouds, for ~15-25% fewer DRAM bits per unit of work; pool operators get a business model.

title: Content-hashed singleton cache for model weights across a rack
idea: Inference hosts each keep 10-30 model checkpoints in host DRAM for fast swapping, mostly the same popular open weights. Hash each 2 MB weight page and keep one physical copy in a rack CXL appliance, mapped read-only into every host; LoRA adapters and private fine-tunes stay local.
why: Host-side model caches shrink 10-30x per rack (N identical copies down to 1), freeing hundreds of GB per server for KV offload or cutting host DRAM purchases.

title: Memory-controller-assisted marking lets GC heaps run near live size
idea: Garbage-collected heaps are sized at 2-3x live data because marking is slow and must stay ahead of allocation. The memory controller keeps a hardware mark bit per 16 B granule in spare ECC metadata and traces references in the background with a pointer-chasing engine, so the runtime can collect continuously and set headroom near 1.2x live.
why: Java, Go, .NET and JS heaps are a large share of cloud DRAM; cutting headroom from ~2.5x to ~1.2x frees 30-50% of that memory.

title: Range-proven bit-precise fields with hardware bitfield load/store
idea: A field holding 0-100 needs 7 bits but is stored in 32 or 64. The compiler proves value ranges (abstract interpretation plus runtime guards) and packs struct fields at bit granularity; new bitfield load/store instructions with extract/insert at the memory side keep access single-cycle and trap on overflow so the layout can widen.
why: 20-40% smaller record-heavy data (in-memory databases, game state, ad features) with no change to algorithms.

title: Rank/select engines enabling succinct trees and graphs in DRAM
idea: Information theory says an n-node tree needs only ~2n bits, yet pointer trees spend ~128n. Add rank/select and balanced-parentheses navigation units next to the memory controller so succinct encodings (LOUDS, BP, Elias-Fano adjacency lists) traverse in O(1) per hop at near-pointer speed.
why: 5-20x smaller indexes, tries, graphs and genomics structures, which are often DRAM-bound.

title: Regenerate weights from PRNG seeds in the HBM base die
idea: A trained weight block can be approximated as a few coefficients times pseudo-random basis vectors. Store, per 8x8 block, a 16-bit LFSR seed and 4 low-bit coefficients; an LFSR array in the HBM logic die regenerates the basis and the weights at read bandwidth, replacing stored bits with deterministic computation.
why: ~3-4 bits per weight effective (4-5x smaller than FP16); spare logic-die compute becomes virtual capacity.

title: Functional pages: page-table entries that point to generators
idea: Much DRAM holds data derivable from a short program: hashed embeddings, lookup tables, procedural textures, constant or zero-filled arrays. Add a page-table entry type whose payload is a generator-kernel ID plus parameters; a near-memory engine synthesizes the requested 64 B line on read and caches it in a small buffer, so the bits are never stored.
why: The bound becomes Kolmogorov complexity, not raw size: TB-scale recommender embedding tables could shrink 10-100x through hash-composed embeddings.

title: Single-copy capability fabric across kernel, driver and framework
idea: In an AI or analytics pipeline, data often sits in 3-5 copies (page cache, user buffer, framework tensor, pinned staging, device memory). Make physical frames capability-owned: storage DMA lands once in a CXL-shared frame, and ownership moves by updating a page-table capability enforced by the IOMMU instead of by memcpy.
why: 2-3x smaller host memory footprint in data loaders and serving stacks, plus less copy energy.

title: Bank-level attention PIM moves KV from HBM to LPDDR
idea: An HBM bit costs ~3x the wafer area of a DDR5 bit (TSVs and yield loss), yet the KV cache only needs bandwidth for one dot product. Put q.k and softmax-weighted v accumulation units at each LPDDR bank, so the KV cache lives in commodity DRAM and only scores and results cross the bus.
why: The same KV capacity for ~1/3 of the wafer area, freeing HBM for weights; internal bank bandwidth exceeds the HBM interface.

title: Phase-shifting jobs to anticorrelate memory peaks in a pool
idea: Provisioning for the sum of peaks instead of the peak of the sum wastes capacity. A scheduler fingerprints each job's memory-over-time curve (batch ETL, training checkpoints, nightly builds) and offsets start times so that peaks interleave, then sizes the shared pool to the measured peak of the sum plus a margin.
why: In mixed fleets the peak of the sum is typically 30-50% below the sum of peaks, and pool DRAM falls by about as much.

title: Position-free KV storage for cross-user chunk dedup
idea: The same RAG documents and system prompts recur across users at different offsets, which defeats prefix caching. Store each chunk's keys before RoPE, under a content hash; apply the rotary rotation for the real position at read time, and run a small learned correction pass over the first few tokens of each chunk to restore cross-chunk attention.
why: In RAG-heavy serving, KV for shared corpora is stored once per cluster instead of once per request: 5-20x less KV capacity.

title: Approximate-grade DRAM bins sold for error-tolerant tensors
idea: Dies that fail retention binning or exceed their redundancy still hold 99.999% good bits. Bin and sell them as approximate-grade modules with a published bad-cell map; the OS maps only error-tolerant pages there (NN activations, media, sketches), and the map steers sign and exponent bits onto known-good columns.
why: Raises usable supply by recovering 5-15% of dies that are now scrapped or down-binned, with no new fab capital.

title: Endurance-budget tiering: unlimited endurance only where writes demand it
idea: From first principles, DRAM's unlimited endurance matters only for frequently written pages, and most resident bytes are written less than once an hour. Per-page write-rate counters in the controller migrate write-cold pages to a cheaper byte-addressable tier with limited endurance (NOR-like or high-bandwidth flash), and the controller enforces wear budgets.
why: If 50-70% of resident bytes are write-cold, DRAM per server can roughly halve while reads stay byte-addressable.

title: Memory Star: federal memory-efficiency label for cloud procurement
idea: Memory demand is working set x replication x headroom, and procurement measures none of the three. A GSA/DoD procurement standard would require vendors to report GB-hours per unit of work on standard benchmarks and give price preference to the top quartile, as ENERGY STAR did for watts.
why: Demand-side policy that pulls compression, dedup and right-sizing across the industry: 10-20% less DRAM fleet-wide over a few procurement cycles.

title: Ever-read bits drive automatic right-sizing of oversized buffers
idea: A byte that is written but never read delivers zero information. The memory controller keeps an ever-read bit per cache line, cleared on allocation; the allocator periodically scans and shrinks ring buffers, caches and pools whose tails are never read, and profilers report never-read bytes to developers.
why: Oversized buffers and caches commonly waste 10-30% of a service's footprint, and telemetry-driven trimming recovers most of it.

title: Experts stored as shared base plus low-rank deltas
idea: MoE experts and per-tenant fine-tunes are highly correlated, so their joint information is far less than N full matrices. Factor each expert as W_base + A_i B_i (rank 32-128) and compute x.W_base + (x.A_i).B_i on the fly, so memory holds one base and N small deltas.
why: 5-10x smaller expert and multi-tenant fine-tune memory, for a few percent extra FLOPs.

title: Fiber-loop weight carousel broadcasting one copy to a hall
idea: Decode reads every weight once per step in a fixed order, so weights need sequential access, not random access. Circulate one copy of a model's weights in a multicore WDM glass-fiber loop (InP lasers, thin-film lithium-niobate modulators, erbium amplifiers, periodic optical regeneration), and let every accelerator tap the passing stream through a passive coupler instead of holding the weights in HBM.
why: One copy in flight serves hundreds of accelerators, so weight HBM per GPU falls toward zero (weights are ~50-70% of inference HBM). Honest cost: per bit-second the loop burns more power than refresh (~0.1 nW vs ~0.7 pW per bit), and a 70B FP8 model at 100 Tb/s needs ~1,100 km of fiber, so it only wins through massive fan-out.

title: Passive optical splitters copy one weight stream to many accelerators
idea: Copying a bit electrically costs CV^2 at every receiver; an optical 1:N splitter copies light passively, down to a shot-noise floor of ~100 photons per bit per receiver. Serve weights from a single pooled memory through polymer waveguides laminated into the organic board with 1:16 splitters, and synchronize the replicas so all of them read the same layer at the same moment.
why: Data-parallel replicas stop holding private weight copies, so weight memory per replica falls up to 16x; each extra receiver costs ~0.1 pJ/bit vs ~1-3 pJ/bit electrically.

title: Display-glass oxide-TFT warm tier priced by area, not wafer
idea: Cost per bit is area x cost per area, and processed display glass costs ~100-1000x less per cm^2 than a DRAM wafer. Build 1T1C arrays on Gen 8.5 glass on existing IGZO backplane lines, with large planar capacitors (no high-aspect-ratio etch) and ~1e-19 A/um leakage for minute-scale retention, packaged as a CXL warm tier at ~200 ns-1 us.
why: Even with a cell 100x larger than silicon DRAM, cost per bit can be ~5-10x lower. Warm pages move there, so silicon DRAM shrinks to the hot set (30-50% less), using idle LCD capacity.

title: Smart-window electrochromic glass as analog weight-stationary crossbars
idea: Ion intercalation in WO3/NiO films, the chemistry of US-made smart windows, holds a non-volatile analog conductance that changes only when ions are driven. Pattern crossbars of these cells on window-glass coating lines, so frozen inference weights sit in place as conductances and matrix-vector products happen through Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws, with no weight bits in DRAM.
why: Frozen weights (~50-70% of inference memory) leave DRAM entirely, at ~fJ per MAC instead of pJ per fetched bit; coating lines in the US help manufacturability. Risks: slow ionic programming and drift.

title: Charge-domain KV attention in glass capacitor arrays
idea: Attention needs dot products, not exactly stored bits. Store each key as analog voltages on TFT capacitors on glass (3-4 effective bits per cell), compute q.k by switched-capacitor charge sharing along the columns, digitize only the top-k scores, and fetch the values for those tokens digitally.
why: The KV cache moves off silicon DRAM into cheap glass area as approximate storage: ~4x fewer bits than FP16, and no KV traffic during the score phase.

title: Glass-panel interposer lets accelerators share one memory set
idea: Weights are replicated per GPU only because off-package bandwidth is too poor to share them. A 510x515 mm glass-core panel interposer with 2 um RDL and through-glass vias places 8 accelerators around one common ring of memory stacks at near-local bandwidth, so tensor- and data-parallel groups read a single physical copy of the weights.
why: Weight replicas per 8-GPU group drop from 8 to 1-2, cutting HBM bits per deployment 30-60%; glass is low-loss and uses no silicon interposer wafers.

title: MicroLED-on-sapphire parallel links make pooled memory nearly free
idea: Pooling saves DRAM only if remote access costs nearly as much as local. GaN microLED and photodiode arrays grown on sapphire, coupled into glass imaging-fiber bundles, carry CXL traffic across a rack over hundreds of slow parallel lanes (~2 Gb/s each, no SerDes) at ~1 pJ/bit and low latency.
why: Makes rack-scale pooling viable even for latency-sensitive tiers, so operators provision ~20-30% less DRAM per server by reclaiming stranded memory.

title: Fused-silica volume holograms hold cold MoE experts
idea: In a large MoE most experts are idle most of the time, yet they occupy HBM. Store them as page-oriented volume holograms in femtosecond-laser-written fused silica or photopolymer on glass, read by a fixed-angle laser array and a detector array that returns a megabit page in ~1-10 us; only experts routed for the next few tokens are staged into HBM.
why: Trillion-parameter MoE needs 3-10x less HBM because only active experts stay resident; glass media cost cents per GB and retain data with zero refresh energy.

title: Photorefractive crystal associative memory prefilters attention keys
idea: Attention is a correlation search, and optics does correlation natively. Record the keys as holographic gratings in an iron-doped lithium-niobate crystal; a query beam diffracts into correlation peaks whose brightness ranks the keys, and only the top-k token positions are fetched from a compressed KV store for exact attention.
why: Full-precision KV no longer has to sit in fast DRAM, because only the top-k (<5%) is read. The KV store can then be compressed or tiered, ~10x less DRAM for million-token contexts.

title: Multimode-fiber speckle hashing finds duplicate pages for free
idea: A multimode glass fiber is a fixed random matrix, so the speckle pattern at its output is a random projection of its input, which is a locality-sensitive hash. Modulate candidate pages or KV chunks onto a laser, send them through the fiber and read a 1-kpixel camera; matching speckle signatures flag exact and near-duplicate content for merging.
why: Background dedup scanning at near-zero silicon cost and energy, including near-duplicate merging (images, KV chunks, embedding rows) that exact hashing misses: 10-30% smaller footprint on VM-dense and serving hosts.

title: Laser-written diffractive glass embodies frozen network layers
idea: A fixed linear transform needs no stored bits if it is built into geometry. Write the frozen embedding projection or the early layers of vision and speech models as stacked phase plates in fused silica (femtosecond direct write); a microLED array encodes the inputs and photodiodes read the outputs, so those weights occupy no DRAM and need no refresh.
why: Weights and activations of frozen front-end layers leave DRAM in edge devices and high-volume serving, and energy per MAC is near zero because propagating light does the work.

title: Roll-to-roll printed ferroelectric polymer read-mostly memory tier
idea: Read-mostly data (embedding tables, checkpoints, search indexes) needs few writes, so 1e7-1e8 cycles of endurance is enough. Gravure-print ferroelectric-diode crossbars from a P(VDF-TrFE):semiconductor blend, which gives a non-destructive resistive read, onto PET film at roll-to-roll speed, and laminate many films into a stack.
why: R2R printing costs ~10,000x less per area than silicon, so even at microsecond access, offloading read-mostly bytes trims DRAM 20-40% in recommender and search fleets.

title: Acoustic delay-line FIFOs buffer pipeline-parallel activations
idea: Pipeline-stage activations and switch packet buffers are strictly first-in-first-out, so they do not need random-access cells. Store them as surface acoustic waves on lithium-niobate or quartz: at ~3.5 km/s a 2 cm line holds ~6 us, and 1,000 parallel 5 GHz channels in recirculating, re-amplified loops hold ~30 Mbit.
why: Frees MB-scale HBM and DRAM buffers in deep-buffer switches and pipeline stages. The capacity is small, but every byte moved out of HBM also avoids its ~3x wafer tax.

title: Piezo-steered fiber switches re-home memory blades by demand
idea: Static wiring between memory and servers forces each server to carry its own peak. Fiber cross-connects steered by piezoceramic actuators (no silicon MEMS) rewire whole memory blades between servers every few seconds to minutes, following the scheduler's demand forecast, with the optical path carrying CXL over fiber.
why: Capacity follows demand at rack-to-row scale, so provisioned DRAM per server drops 20-35%, and an attached blade still delivers local latency and full bandwidth.

title: IGZO panel sums embedding rows in place by current mode
idea: Recommender inference gathers dozens of embedding rows only to sum them, so only the sum matters. Store the embedding tables in IGZO 2T gain cells on display glass and activate every row of a lookup batch at once, so read currents add on shared column lines and a column ADC returns the pooled vector directly.
why: TB-scale embedding tables move from silicon DRAM onto glass, and only one vector per lookup crosses the link (20-80x less traffic).

title: Million slow TFT compressors on glass for cold pages
idea: Compressing cold pages is bound by throughput, not latency, so slow transistors suffice if there are enough of them. Tile a glass panel with ~1 million LTPS-TFT LZ/rANS engines at ~1-5 MHz each (aggregate >1e12 symbol operations/s), fed through optical I/O, which compress cold pages in the background and write them back to DRAM compacted.
why: Every server gets zswap-class 2-3x compression of cold memory without spending CPU cycles or silicon logic area.

title: Bit-plane split: MSBs in silicon, LSBs on glass
idea: The bits of a weight or activation differ in importance by powers of two, so they need not share a medium. Keep sign, exponent and top mantissa bits in silicon DRAM and the low mantissa planes in a glass-TFT tier with relaxed retention and no ECC; both are read in parallel and recombined on the fly, and LSB errors cost little accuracy.
why: Silicon DRAM per tensor drops 40-60% at negligible accuracy loss, with cheap approximate glass bits holding the low-value half.

title: Oxide-TFT leakage as a built-in forgetting curve for KV
idea: For most heads, attention decays with distance, so old tokens can fade instead of being refreshed. Store low-priority KV heads on glass TFT capacitors whose leakage is tuned per bank (channel length, gate bias) to a chosen time constant, and have the sense circuit treat faded entries as zero.
why: Zero refresh energy and automatic eviction with no bookkeeping; these heads, roughly 30-50% of KV in long-context models, need no silicon DRAM at all.

title: Advance purchase commitment for US-made glass memory tiers
idea: Federal buyers (DOE labs, DoD, GSA cloud) pre-commit to buy, for example, 500 PB over 5 years of CXL warm-tier memory built on non-silicon substrates at a target of <$1/GB, paid on delivery. This lets US glass makers and idle display lines finance conversion without silicon fab capital.
why: Removes demand risk from a substrate path that needs no EUV, no helium-intensive crystal pulling and no Spruce Pine quartz crucibles, and builds US memory supply outside the DRAM oligopoly.

title: Planar thin-film magnetic cores on glass revive core memory
idea: Core memory was byte-addressable, had unlimited endurance and needed no refresh; it lost only on size. Pattern micro-toroids of electroplated permalloy or ferrite with multi-turn copper windings on glass panels using panel-level packaging lithography (~10 um features), select them by coincident-current half-select and sense them inductively at ~100-300 ns.
why: A warm tier with no refresh and no wear, made in the US on panel-packaging tools; it can hold write-heavy warm data that flash tiers cannot, relieving silicon DRAM.

title: Hollow-core fiber widens memory-pooling radius by 45 percent
idea: Remote-memory latency is bounded by the speed of light in the medium: ~5 ns/m in solid glass, ~3.4 ns/m in hollow-core fiber. Wire memory pools with hollow-core fiber so a 300 ns round-trip budget reaches ~47% farther, roughly doubling the floor area, and so the number of servers, that one pool can cover.
why: Pool headroom scales roughly as 1/sqrt(N), so doubling the servers per pool trims another ~5-10% of provisioned DRAM.

title: Memory-in-pixel panels absorb the framebuffer out of DRAM
idea: A display backplane already is a memory: every pixel has a TFT and a storage capacitor on glass. Put a 1-3 bit latch or oxide-TFT gain cell in each subpixel (memory-in-pixel) and composite static layers directly in the panel, so phones, laptops and VR headsets stop keeping triple-buffered framebuffers and static layers in DRAM.
why: Frees 100-500 MB per device (4K-8K, multiple layers, triple buffering) plus the refresh traffic; small per device, but across billions of units.

title: Rotating nanostructured glass platter streams weights to batch inference
idea: In throughput-oriented batch inference the weight pass is a sequential scan of read-only data, which rotating media serve at the lowest cost per bit. A spinning fused-silica platter with laser-written multilevel nanostructures is read by a 10,000-element VCSEL/photodiode head array (~1 Gb/s each, ~10 Tb/s total), streaming a 70B FP8 model every ~60 ms, amortized over a batch of hundreds of sequences.
why: Weights leave DRAM entirely for batch jobs; the glass medium costs <$0.01/GB and needs no power to retain data.
